nameStory: Long's Bittercress gets its name from botanist William Henry Long, who first identified this distinctive species. The "bitter" part comes from the sharp, peppery taste of its leaves - similar to watercress but with more bite. Like other bittercresses, it belongs to the mustard family, which explains that characteristic spicy flavor that tingles on your tongue.
description: Long's Bittercress is a small, delicate wildflower that most people walk right past without noticing. This slender annual grows only 4-8 inches tall, with tiny white flowers clustered at the top of thin stems. Its leaves are deeply divided into narrow segments, giving the plant a feathery, almost fern-like appearance. Despite its small size, this little mustard family member packs a peppery punch if you dare to taste a leaf.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided leaves with 3-7 narrow, linear segments that feel smooth and slightly succulent when rubbed between your fingers. The leaves taste distinctly peppery and sharp, much like arugula but more intense.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers, barely 1/8 inch across, with four petals arranged in a cross pattern typical of mustard family plants. They cluster at the tips of slender stems and have a faint, sweet fragrance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing annual that forms small rosettes at the base with upright flowering stems reaching 4-8 inches tall. The plant feels delicate and breaks easily when handled.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Narrow, upright seed pods (called siliques) about 1/2 inch long that split open explosively when ripe, shooting seeds several feet away with an audible 'pop' when touched.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, smooth, light green stems that are slightly angular rather than perfectly round. They snap crisply when bent and have a mild peppery scent when crushed.

habitat: Long's Bittercress favors moist, disturbed soils in partially shaded areas throughout New England's lowlands and foothills. Look for it along stream banks, in wet meadows, and at the edges of woodland paths where the soil stays consistently damp. It often grows alongside other moisture-loving plants like violets and wild ginger in rich, organic soils.

seasonality.spring: Flowers appear in late April through May, producing their tiny white cross-shaped blooms. Young leaves are most tender and flavorful for tasting during this season.
seasonality.summer: Seed pods develop and ripen by mid-summer, becoming explosive to the touch. Plants may die back in hot, dry weather but can produce a second flush of growth if moisture returns.
seasonality.fall: Often produces a second generation of plants that flower again in early fall if conditions are favorable. Seeds from spring plants germinate to form small rosettes.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely as an annual, leaving only seeds in the soil to germinate the following spring. No above-ground parts remain visible.

funFact: Long's Bittercress has explosive seed pods that can launch their seeds up to 6 feet away with enough force to make an audible popping sound - it's like nature's own tiny cannons going off when you brush against a ripe plant!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small bittercresses, especially Pennsylvania Bittercress which grows in similar habitats. Long's Bittercress has more deeply divided leaves with narrower segments, while Pennsylvania Bittercress has broader, less divided leaflets. Remember: "Long's has long, narrow leaf segments."
contextualKnowledge: Long's Bittercress is considered quite rare in New England, with only a few confirmed sightings. Some botanists debate whether it's truly distinct from other bittercresses or just a variation, which explains why it's so seldom reported. If you think you've found it, consider photographing it and reporting to local botanists.
compareHints: Long's Bittercress differs from its relatives by having the most finely divided leaves in the genus - almost thread-like compared to the broader leaflets of Two-leaved Toothwort or the simpler leaves of Hairy Bittercress. While Cuckooflower has pink flowers and grows much larger, Long's stays tiny with pure white blooms. The explosive seed pods are shared with most bittercresses, but Long's narrow leaf segments make it distinctive when in vegetative form.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's toothworts and bittercresses, two-leaved toothwort is unique for its simple three-parted leaves and paired leaf arrangement.
Among New England's bittercresses, hairy bittercress is distinguished by its small size, annual habit, and compound leaves with rounded leaflets.

Among its bittercress relatives, narrow-leaved bittercress stands out for its particularly slender, lance-shaped leaflets—much narrower than the rounded leaflets of hairy bittercress or the broader segments of Pennsylvania bittercress.
Among New England's bittercresses, Pennsylvania bittercress stands out for its smooth leaves and taller stature.
Among New England's toothworts, cut-leaved stands out with its three deeply-divided leaves arranged in a whorl, while two-leaved toothwort has just two broader, less-divided leaves.
Among its Cardamine relatives in New England, cuckooflower stands out for preferring wetter habitats than most bittercresses and toothworts.
Among its many Cardamine relatives in New England, bulbous cress stands out for its underground bulb and preference for very wet soils.
Among New England's bittercresses, nursery bittercress is distinguished by its completely smooth leaves and preference for disturbed garden soils.
Large toothwort differs from its close relative cut-leaved toothwort by having more finely divided, almost lacy leaflets and typically growing taller.
Among its bittercress relatives, sand bittercress is distinguished by its preference for sandy, dry soils and its particularly small size.

Alpine bittercress is dramatically different from its lowland Cardamine relatives in New England - while species like hairy bittercress and Pennsylvania bittercress are weedy annuals that pop up in gardens and disturbed areas, alpine bittercress is a specialized perennial that grows only in extreme mountain conditions.

Among its Cardamine relatives in New England, Purple Cress is unique for its potential purple flower coloration - species like Two-leaved Toothwort and the various bittercresses typically stick to white or pale pink flowers.

Among the Cardamine genus in New England, white cuckoo bitter-cress has the most finely divided, feathery leaves - much more delicate than the broader leaflets of toothworts or the simpler leaves of other bitter-cresses.
Chinese Ivy differs from other Cardamine species in New England by being strictly aquatic and having a trailing, mat-forming growth habit.
